questions.stem: Which of these surfaces reflects the largest fraction of the sunlight that falls on it?
options: Open ocean
Dark forest
Bare soil
Fresh snow
questions.explanation: Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight that reaches it, so its albedo is very high. Open ocean has one of the lowest albedos of any surface, absorbing most of the sunlight that falls on it.

questions.stem: Sunlight delivers 800 W/m2 to a snowfield with an albedo of 0.85. How much energy does each square metre absorb?
questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction reflected, so 0.85 x 800 = 680 W/m2 is reflected and 800 - 680 = 120 W/m2 is absorbed. The value 680 W/m2 is the reflected energy, not the absorbed energy.

questions.stem: Earth's average albedo is about 0.3. What does this mean for Earth's energy budget?
options: About 30% of incoming sunlight is reflected and about 70% is absorbed
About 30% of incoming sunlight is absorbed and about 70% is reflected
About 30% of Earth's surface is covered by ice that reflects sunlight
About 30% of Earth's heat is lost to space, mostly through the oceans
questions.explanation: An albedo of 0.3 means 30% of incoming solar radiation is reflected by clouds, air, aerosols and the surface. The remaining 70% is absorbed and warms the Earth, so overall Earth is more an absorber than a reflector.

questions.stem: During past ice ages, ice sheets spread across North America and Europe. How did albedo help the cooling continue once the ice began to grow?
options: Ice absorbed more sunlight, so the air above warmed and ice kept forming
Ice trapped more infrared radiation, so the surface lost less heat overall
Ice released stored heat as it formed, so the oceans cooled more quickly
Ice reflected more sunlight, so less was absorbed and cooling increased
questions.explanation: Growing ice replaces darker land and sea, raising albedo, so more sunlight is reflected and the surface cools further, which allows more ice to form. This is a positive feedback. Melting ice works the same way in reverse, speeding up warming.

questions.stem: A large area of dark eucalypt forest is cleared and replaced by pale, dry pasture. Considering albedo alone, how would the local surface energy balance change?
options: The same sunlight is reflected, as albedo depends only on clouds
More sunlight is reflected, so less is absorbed at the surface
Less sunlight is reflected, so more is absorbed at the surface
No sunlight is reflected, so all of it is absorbed by the soil
questions.explanation: Pale, dry grass has a higher albedo than dark forest, so it reflects a larger share of sunlight. Other effects of clearing, such as less evaporation and carbon released from the trees, can outweigh this, which is why albedo alone does not decide the net effect.

questions.stem: Which gases are examples of greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere?
options: Oxygen, ozone, hydrogen and helium in the upper atmosphere
Nitrogen, argon, neon and helium from volcanic outgassing
Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
Nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide in equal amounts
questions.explanation: Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all absorb infrared radiation. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon make up about 99% of dry air but do not absorb infrared significantly.

questions.stem: After a carbon dioxide molecule in the lower atmosphere absorbs infrared radiation from the ground, what happens to that energy?
options: It is stored permanently, so the molecule becomes hotter forever
It is turned into visible light, which is reflected by clouds
It is re-emitted in all directions, so some returns to the surface
It is re-emitted only upwards, so all of it escapes into space
questions.explanation: The molecule re-emits infrared radiation in every direction and also shares energy with nearby air molecules by collision. Because part of the radiation goes back down, the surface and lower atmosphere are warmer than they would be otherwise.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the greenhouse effect?
options: Sunlight is absorbed by gases; gases cool the surface; the surface absorbs infrared from space
Sunlight warms the surface; the surface emits infrared; gases absorb and re-emit some back
Infrared from the Sun warms gases; gases emit visible light; the surface reflects it to space
Gases reflect sunlight downwards; the surface absorbs it; the surface stops emitting energy
questions.explanation: Most sunlight passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the surface, which then emits longer-wavelength infrared. Greenhouse gases absorb much of this and re-emit part of it back down, reducing heat loss to space.

questions.stem: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be well below freezing. Why does this matter for the hydrosphere and biosphere?
options: It removes water vapour from the air, preventing all rainfall
It stops sunlight reaching the surface, protecting life from UV
It keeps most surface water liquid, which life depends on
It keeps the oceans frozen, which protects life from storms
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect raises the average surface temperature to about 15 °C, so most water stays liquid, supporting the water cycle and living things. The problem today is the enhanced effect from added greenhouse gases, not the natural effect itself.

questions.stem: Why does a cloudless desert night become cold much faster than a humid tropical night?
options: Desert sand has a low albedo at night, so it absorbs cold from the air
Desert air is denser, so it sinks and pushes warm air away from the ground
Dry air holds little water vapour, so less infrared is absorbed and returned
Dry air holds more carbon dioxide, so it reflects heat back out to space
questions.explanation: Water vapour is a powerful greenhouse gas. With little of it in dry desert air, more of the infrared emitted by the ground escapes straight to space, so the surface cools rapidly. Albedo concerns reflected sunlight, which plays no part at night.

questions.stem: Why does air above a strongly heated surface rise?
options: It loses water vapour and becomes heavier than cool air
It gains oxygen from the ground and becomes more buoyant
It expands and becomes less dense than the air around it
It contracts and becomes denser than the air around it
questions.explanation: Heated air expands, so the same mass occupies more volume and its density falls. Denser surrounding air sinks and pushes it upward, setting up a convection current. Cooler air aloft later sinks to complete the loop.

questions.stem: Why is there a net transfer of heat from the tropics towards the poles in the atmosphere?
options: The tropics have more ice, which releases heat into the air as it melts
The poles have more greenhouse gases, which draw heat from the equator
The tropics receive more solar energy per square metre than they lose
The poles receive more solar energy per square metre than the tropics
questions.explanation: Near the equator, sunlight strikes almost vertically, concentrating energy on a small area, so the tropics have an energy surplus while high latitudes have a deficit. Circulating air (and ocean currents) carries heat poleward, which is why the tropics do not keep heating up.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric convection cell lies between the equator and about 30 degrees latitude?
options: The Walker cell
The Hadley cell
The Ferrel cell
The polar cell
questions.explanation: In the Hadley cell, air rises near the equator, moves poleward aloft, sinks near 30 degrees and returns to the equator as the trade winds. The Ferrel cell lies between about 30 and 60 degrees, and the polar cell from 60 degrees to the pole.

questions.stem: Which belt of weather is caused by air rising where the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet near the equator?
options: A belt of heavy rain and thunderstorms
A belt of dry, clear, cloudless skies
A belt of strong, steady westerly winds
A belt of cold air and frequent snowfall
questions.explanation: Air converging and rising near the equator cools, and its water vapour condenses, producing towering clouds and heavy rain. This is why tropical rainforests lie near the equator. Dry skies occur where air sinks, near 30 degrees.

questions.stem: Adelaide gets most of its rain in winter, from cold fronts, and little in summer. How does the movement of the global cells with the seasons explain this?
options: In summer the polar cell moves north over the city, bringing cold dry air from Antarctica
In summer the Hadley cell moves south over the city, bringing rising air and frequent rain
In winter the high-pressure belt moves north, letting fronts in the westerlies reach the city
In winter the high-pressure belt moves south, letting the moist trade winds reach the city
questions.explanation: The belt of sinking air and high pressure near 30 degrees south shifts north in winter and south in summer. In winter this lets the westerly winds of the Ferrel cell, with their cold fronts, reach southern Australia. In summer high pressure sits over the region and blocks them.

questions.stem: Students heat one side of a tank of water containing a drop of dye. The dye rises above the heat, moves across the top, sinks at the cool side and returns along the bottom. Which atmospheric feature does this best model?
options: The greenhouse effect warming the surface
The albedo of clouds reflecting sunlight
A convection cell, such as the Hadley cell
The Coriolis effect deflecting the winds
questions.explanation: The loop of rising warm fluid, sideways flow, sinking cool fluid and return flow is a convection cell, like the Hadley cell with its rising air near the equator and sinking air near 30 degrees. The model has no rotation, so it cannot show the Coriolis effect.

questions.stem: What causes the Coriolis effect?
options: Earth's tilted axis
Earth's orbit of the Sun
The pull of the Moon
Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: Because Earth rotates, points at different latitudes move east at different speeds, so freely moving air or water appears to be deflected relative to the ground. Earth's tilt causes the seasons, not the Coriolis effect.

questions.stem: Air moving towards the equator in the Southern Hemisphere's Hadley cell is deflected by the Coriolis effect. From which direction do these trade winds blow?
options: From the south-east
From the north-east
From the south-west
From the north-west
questions.explanation: Air flowing north towards the equator is deflected to its left in the Southern Hemisphere, which is towards the west, so it blows from the south-east. The north-east trades are the Northern Hemisphere's equivalent.

questions.stem: Tropical cyclones almost never form within about 5 degrees of the equator, even where the sea is very warm. Why?
options: The sea there is too salty to evaporate and supply the storm
The trade winds there blow from the poles and are too cold
The Coriolis effect is too weak there to start the air spinning
The Coriolis effect is strongest there, so it tears storms apart
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect is zero at the equator and increases towards the poles. A cyclone needs some deflection to organise the inflowing air into a rotating system, so near the equator storms cannot spin up.

questions.stem: In the Southern Hemisphere's Ferrel cell, surface air moves from about 30 degrees towards 60 degrees south. After the Coriolis effect acts, which winds result?
options: Easterlies, blowing from the south-east and east
Northerlies, blowing straight from the equator
Southerlies, blowing straight from Antarctica
Westerlies, blowing from the north-west and west
questions.explanation: Air moving south is deflected to its left, which is towards the east, so it blows from the west or north-west. These are the westerlies of the 'Roaring Forties', which carry cold fronts across southern Australia.

questions.stem: An unguided projectile is launched due north from Hobart towards Darwin. Relative to the ground, why does it drift slightly west?
options: It is pulled west by the Sun's gravity, which is strongest over the tropics
It is pushed west by the ocean currents, which flow fastest below the equator
It keeps the slower eastward speed of higher latitudes as the ground beneath moves faster
It gains extra eastward speed from the air, so the ground falls behind it to the west
questions.explanation: Points nearer the equator travel further each day as Earth spins, so they move east faster. An object leaving a higher latitude carries its slower eastward speed, so the ground beneath gets ahead of it and it drifts west, a deflection to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.stem: Moist south-easterly winds from the Coral Sea rise over the ranges near the north Queensland coast. Why are the eastern slopes covered in rainforest while land to the west is much drier?
options: Rising air warms and holds its moisture until it reaches the drier inland side
Sinking air cools and carries extra moisture to the inland side of the ranges
Rising air cools and drops its rain on the windward side, leaving a rain shadow
Sinking air warms and drops its rain on the windward side, leaving a rain shadow
questions.explanation: Air forced up the ranges expands and cools, so water vapour condenses and falls as rain on the windward slopes, supporting rainforest. The air descending on the far side warms and dries, so the lee side lies in a rain shadow with drier woodland.

questions.stem: In summer, hot, dry northerly winds from the interior sometimes blow across Adelaide ahead of a cold front. How do they affect local ecosystems?
options: They raise fire danger and heat stress, drying out vegetation and soils
They bring heavy rain that floods wetlands and helps seedlings to grow
They lower temperatures sharply, so frost damages native vegetation
They carry sea salt inland, so coastal plants spread far into the hills
questions.explanation: Continental air from the dry interior is hot and has very low humidity, so it dries out fuels and plants, stresses animals and raises bushfire danger. The cold front behind it brings the cooler, moister air from the Southern Ocean.

questions.stem: Perth and Brisbane lie at similar latitudes, but Perth has dry summers and winter rain while Brisbane has wet summers. Which explanation fits best?
options: Perth is closer to the equator, so its rain falls in winter from monsoon winds from the north
Perth has more greenhouse gases over it, so its summer rain evaporates before reaching the ground
Brisbane gets moist onshore trades and warm seas in summer; Perth lies under summer high pressure
Brisbane lies under the summer high-pressure belt; Perth gets moist trade winds from the Pacific
questions.explanation: In summer, warm seas and onshore easterly trades bring moisture to Queensland's east coast. Perth, on the west coast, sits under the subtropical high in summer, with sinking dry air, and gets rain in winter from fronts in the westerlies, a Mediterranean pattern.

questions.stem: As dry air descends the lee side of a mountain range, it warms and becomes even drier, a 'foehn' or 'Chinook' wind. Why does the descending air warm?
options: It releases latent heat as water vapour freezes to form ice
It is compressed as air pressure increases at lower altitudes
It is heated by contact with the warm snow on the mountain tops
It absorbs extra sunlight because dry air has a high albedo
questions.explanation: Air pressure rises as air descends, so the air is compressed and its temperature increases. Having lost moisture as rain on the windward side, it arrives on the lee side warm and dry, raising fire risk and drying soils.

questions.stem: In normal (neutral) conditions, how do the trade winds affect surface water in the tropical Pacific Ocean?
options: They push warm water east, piling it up along the coast of South America
They push cold water north, piling it up near Japan and the Philippines
They push warm water south, piling it up around New Zealand and Antarctica
They push warm water west, piling it up near Indonesia and Australia
questions.explanation: The easterly trades drag warm surface water westward, building a warm pool in the western Pacific. Off South America cold, deep water rises to replace it. During El Niño, the trades weaken and warm water spreads back east.

questions.stem: During an El Niño, why do fish catches often fall sharply off the coast of Peru?
options: Cold surface water increases the upwelling, so fish swim to warmer areas
Stronger trade winds blow the fishing fleets far out into the Pacific
Heavier rain over Peru washes so much fresh water into the sea that fish die
Warm surface water reduces the upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water
questions.explanation: Normally upwelling brings nutrients from deep water to the surface, supporting plankton and huge fish populations. During El Niño, warm water spreads across the eastern Pacific and upwelling weakens, so productivity and fish catches fall.

questions.stem: During El Niño, a small weakening of the trade winds lets warm water move east, which weakens the east-west temperature difference, which weakens the trade winds further. What does this show?
options: The Coriolis effect causes El Niño by reversing the trades
The ocean and atmosphere are coupled in a positive feedback
The ocean controls the atmosphere, but never the reverse
The atmosphere and ocean change independently of each other
questions.explanation: Each change reinforces the other: weaker winds warm the east, and a warmer east weakens the winds. This coupling is why ENSO events grow and persist for months. It is not one-way control, and the Coriolis effect does not reverse the trades.

questions.stem: Why does an El Niño often increase bushfire risk in south-eastern Australia?
options: Rainfall is often above average, so grasses grow and then flood
Winds are often calmer, so lightning strikes become more common
Temperatures are often cooler, so frost kills more vegetation
Rainfall is often below average, so vegetation and soils dry out
questions.explanation: With the warm pool and rising air shifted east, less moisture reaches eastern Australia, so winter and spring rainfall is often below average and days are warmer. Dry fuels raise bushfire danger the following summer.

questions.stem: El Niño and La Niña events recur at irregular intervals, roughly every two to seven years. What does this mean for forecasting?
options: Events cannot be forecast at all, so ocean monitoring of the Pacific is not useful
Events always alternate, so a La Niña must follow every El Niño the next year
Events must be forecast from current ocean and air observations, not a fixed timetable
Events can be forecast years in advance by counting forward from the last event
questions.explanation: Because ENSO is not a regular cycle, forecasters use buoys, satellites and climate models to watch sea temperatures, winds and pressure, and predict a few months ahead. Neutral years can follow either phase, so events do not simply alternate.

questions.stem: A strong La Niña develops. Which combination of effects is most likely?
options: Below-average rain in Indonesia, and a weaker warm pool in the western Pacific
Above-average rain and flooding in eastern Australia, and cooler water off Peru
Drought in eastern Australia, and warmer water and heavy rain along Peru's coast
No change in Australian rainfall, but much stronger cyclones near South America
questions.explanation: La Niña strengthens the normal pattern: stronger trades pile more warm water in the west, so eastern Australia and Indonesia are wetter, while upwelling off Peru intensifies and the water there cools. Drought in eastern Australia is typical of El Niño.

questions.stem: Water mass P is at 2 °C with a salinity of 35 g/kg. Water mass Q is at 20 °C with a salinity of 35 g/kg. Water mass R is at 2 °C with a salinity of 34 g/kg. Which is densest and most likely to sink?
options: P
Q
R
Q and R equally
questions.explanation: Colder and saltier water is denser. P and R are equally cold, but P is saltier, so P is denser than R. Q has the same salinity as P but is much warmer, so it is the least dense of the three.

questions.stem: Large amounts of fresh meltwater from Greenland's ice sheet flow into the far North Atlantic. Why might this slow the global-ocean conveyor belt?
options: Meltwater is warmer than seawater, so it heats the deep ocean and stops currents
Meltwater adds extra salt from the rocks, so the surface water becomes too heavy
Fresher surface water is less dense, so less of it sinks to form deep water
Fresher surface water is more dense, so it sinks too quickly and blocks the flow
questions.explanation: The conveyor is driven partly by cold, salty surface water sinking in the North Atlantic. Freshwater lowers salinity and density, so less water sinks, weakening the deep flow and the return of warm surface water northward.

questions.stem: Ireland and the Labrador coast of Canada lie at similar latitudes, yet Ireland's winters are far milder. What is the main reason?
options: Ireland has a lower albedo, because it is covered in snow for more of the winter
Warm surface water carried north-east by the conveyor belt warms the air over Ireland
Cold deep water carried south by the conveyor belt warms the air over Ireland by upwelling
Ireland is closer to the equator, so it receives far more solar energy in winter
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift, the surface limb of the conveyor, carry tropical heat towards north-western Europe, and westerly winds bring that warmth onshore. Labrador is bathed by a cold current flowing south from the Arctic instead.

questions.stem: Why is deep water that has travelled along the conveyor belt for centuries rich in nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate?
options: Volcanic rocks dissolve in it and release nitrate from the crust
Dead organisms sink into it and decompose, releasing nutrients
Sunlight reaches the deep ocean and makes plankton grow there
Rivers flow directly into the deep ocean along the sea floor
questions.explanation: Organisms die in the sunlit surface layer and sink, and bacteria in the deep water decompose them, releasing nutrients. With no light for photosynthesis, the nutrients are not used up at depth. Where this water upwells, it fertilises the surface and supports high productivity.

questions.stem: Cold, dense water sinking in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica carries dissolved carbon dioxide into the deep ocean. Why is this important in the carbon cycle?
options: Sinking water carries CO2 into the mantle, where it stays until volcanoes erupt millions of years later
Cold water dissolves more CO2, and the deep ocean stores it away from the air for centuries
Cold water dissolves less CO2, so sinking water releases its carbon into the air at the poles
Deep water turns dissolved CO2 directly into limestone, removing it from all cycles instantly
questions.explanation: Gases dissolve better in cold water, so high-latitude surface water takes up carbon dioxide, and when it sinks the carbon is isolated from the atmosphere until the water upwells, often after hundreds of years. This makes the deep ocean a major carbon store.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the global-ocean conveyor belt?
options: A belt of warm water along the equator that stays in one place throughout the year
A slow global loop of deep thermohaline currents and wind-driven surface currents
A fast surface current that circles Antarctica, driven only by the westerly winds
A daily rise and fall of the sea surface caused by the pull of the Moon and Sun
questions.explanation: The conveyor links deep currents, driven by differences in temperature and salinity, with surface currents driven by wind. Water may take around a thousand years to complete the loop. The current circling Antarctica is only one part of the system, and tides are a different process.
